children: By Anoop Menon

The current geopolitical environment has reinforced the importance of energy security across the UAE and the wider Gulf, but investment decisions are also being driven by long-term economic diversification and rising electricity demand, according to Khalid Salem, President – Middle East, Mitsubishi Power EMEA.

Investments in advanced manufacturing, digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence (AI), data centres, logistics, tourism and industrial development are increasing electricity demand, making reliable power supply increasingly important to economic competitiveness, he told Zawya Projects.

Salem said the trend is reshaping investment priorities, with governments and utilities focusing on reliable, scalable technologies that support decarbonisation, alongside greater emphasis on supply-chain resilience, local manufacturing and skills development.

“In this context, energy security is no longer simply about access to fuel. It is about building a diversified, flexible and resilient power system that can support economic growth, integrate increasing amounts of renewable energy and respond to evolving demand patterns,” he said.

For the UAE and the wider Gulf, this is driving the need for a balanced energy mix comprising renewables, efficient gas-fired generation, grid infrastructure and energy storage, alongside the longer-term development of lower-carbon fuels such as hydrogen, he noted.

Over the next five to 10 years, Salem expects the Gulf’s power generation mix to become increasingly diversified with renewable energy, particularly large-scale solar, playing a central role in this transition. However, gas-fired generation will continue to play an important role in maintaining system reliability as the share of variable renewable energy increases, he said.

“As more renewable capacity comes online, countries will require flexible, dispatchable power that can respond quickly to changes in supply and demand,” he said. “High-efficiency gas turbines can provide that flexibility, helping to balance variable renewable generation, support grid stability and ensure reliable power for industrial growth, digital infrastructure and emerging demand from sectors such as AI and data centres.”

He also assured that the company’s project execution timelines, procurement strategies and long-term service commitments across the Middle East and Gulf have remained on track despite the current regional conflict.

“This is due in large part to the resilience, agility and dedication of our teams across the region, particularly here in the UAE,” said Salem. “Through proactive planning, strong supplier relationships, and close collaboration with our customers, we have continued to deliver projects and meet our obligations under long-term service agreements [LTSAs].”
Excerpts from the interview
How has the surge in electricity demand, driven by AI/data centres, economic diversification, and population growth, influenced Mitsubishi Power’s outlook for the GCC markets?

The IEA recently forecast that electricity consumption across the MENA region could rise by around 50 percent by 2035. This represents a structural step-change in energy demand, driven by population growth, industrialisation and national economic diversification and decarbonisation strategies.
Above all, however, it is being accelerated by the rapid expansion of AI and data centre infrastructure, as GCC countries position themselves at the heart of the global digital economy.

The scale of this ambition is reflected in landmark digital infrastructure initiatives across the region. For example, the UAE’s 5 GW Stargate AI project and Saudi Arabia’s 6.6 GW HUMAIN data centre roadmap are expected to introduce substantial new base load demand to regional power systems.

In this context, the challenge for the Middle East is no longer simply about adding generation capacity. It is about building energy systems, in many cases almost from the ground up, that combine resilience, flexibility, efficiency and long-term future readiness. Meeting these growing load requirements will require a balanced approach that integrates rapidly expanding renewable energy capacity with highly efficient, flexible dispatchable power solutions.

At Mitsubishi Power, we are excited by the scale of this opportunity and have invested significantly in the region through local facilities, manufacturing capability and skills development. This commitment is reflected in major projects across the GCC, including high-efficiency GTCC technology deployments at the 2,400 MW Fujairah F3 plant in the UAE, our long-term grid reliability upgrades for Kuwait’s Ministry of Electricity, Water and Renewable Energy at the Az-Zour South and Sabiya power stations, and our hydrogen-ready M501JAC gas turbine and long-term service agreement for the SATORP Strategic Expansion power plant in Saudi Arabia.
How important is gas-fired generation in balancing decarbonisation with rising base load demand from sectors such as AI, advanced manufacturing and desalination?
Countries across the GCC are moving at pace to build the economies of the future.
While this varies from market to market, these economies are fundamentally being shaped by the expansion of renewable energy, advanced digital infrastructure, AI and next-generation manufacturing.
All of these sectors depend on one critical foundation: reliable, stable power systems.

In this context, gas plays a critical role. It provides both the dependable baseload power needed to support economic growth while also delivering the flexibility required to balance intermittent renewable generation. Our flagship JAC-series GTCC technology is engineered specifically for this dynamic environment, delivering industry-leading efficiency of more than 64 percent alongside rapid-ramping flexibility that can quickly compensate for the natural fluctuations of expanding solar networks.
How is the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure and hyperscale data centres changing electricity demand patterns in the UAE and the Gulf region?
The change we're witnessing is unprecedented.

Globally, data centres consumed about 415 TWh of electricity in 2024, representing around 1.5 percent of total electricity demand. That figure is already significant, but it is expected to more than double by 2030 as AI adoption accelerates. The same trend is now emerging across the Middle East. In the UAE for example, data centre power consumption is projected to double by 2030.

This is taking place at a time when electricity demand is already rising across the GCC. However, AI, combined with the region’s ambition to become a global leader in the digital economy, has fundamentally changed the scale and complexity of the challenge.

Meeting this demand will require substantial investment in new generation capacity, grid infrastructure and cooling systems. The response, however, cannot be limited to adding capacity alone. AI and hyperscale data centre workloads can be highly variable, placing new demands on grid stability, flexibility and system responsiveness.

That is why the region needs a system-wide approach, one that can accommodate these evolving demand patterns while ensuring reliability and resilience across the power system, without compromising energy security or economic competitiveness.
How do you view the development of next-generation flexible power solutions, including battery storage integration, fast-ramping turbines and hydrogen co-firing systems?

The combination of growing power demand, evolving consumption patterns and the rapid deployment of intermittent renewable energy means that flexibility is becoming a fundamental requirement for power systems in the Middle East. Given the scale of this challenge, it will require an “all of the above” approach that brings together multiple technologies to deliver the reliability, resilience and responsiveness that modern grids demand.

Battery energy storage systems will play a critical role, particularly in providing short-duration flexibility, grid balancing and renewable integration. However, batteries alone cannot address every system requirement. Hydrogen-ready gas turbines offer both the fast-ramping, dispatchable power needed to meet rising demand today, while also providing a clear pathway to lower-carbon power generation for tomorrow.

Mitsubishi Power is a leader in the development of hydrogen-capable gas turbine technologies and its deployment in real-world applications. For example, Georgia Power and Mitsubishi Power successfully validated a 50 percent hydrogen fuel blend on an advanced-class M501GAC gas turbine at Plant McDonough-Atkinson in the United States, marking the first validation of a 50 percent hydrogen blend on an advanced-class gas turbine and the largest demonstration of its kind to date.

In Egypt, we recently completed the conversion of an industrial steam boiler at the Alexandria National Refining and Petrochemicals Company (ANRPC) to operate on 100 percent hydrogen fuel. Described as the first industrial application of hydrogen as fuel in an industrial boiler in Egypt and the MENA region, the project demonstrates that hydrogen is moving beyond demonstrations and into commercial-scale industrial use.

What’s more, all of Mitsubishi Power’s advanced-class gas turbines are hydrogen-ready, including the units recently delivered to the Fujairah F3 power plant in the UAE and the Layyah power plant in Sharjah. These technologies enable the Gulf region to meet its near-term need for flexible, reliable power while creating a practical and scalable pathway toward lower-carbon generation over the long term.

A Wood McKenzie report in April stated that global orders sat at 110 gigawatts (GW) at the end of 2025, but global manufacturing capacity is only capable of 60-70 GW. What factors are driving this demand, and how sustainable do you believe they are from your perspective? How is Mitsubishi Power planning to address this demand-supply gap?

Globally, there are two primary drivers: AI-related growth in electricity demand and the ongoing electrification of economies. In the GCC, these trends are reinforced further by population growth, industrialisation, and national economic diversification and decarbonisation strategies.

These are structural, long-term trends rather than a short-term spike in demand. In this context, high-efficiency gas generation has an important role to play by providing the reliable, flexible power needed to support continued growth while maintaining grid stability.

At Mitsubishi Power, we are addressing the global supply-demand gap through the expansion of manufacturing capacity and continuous improvements across our production processes. At the same time, we are working closely with operators and utilities to extend asset lifetimes, improve availability, optimise performance, and ensure existing plants continue to provide reliable capacity while new projects are being delivered. Much of this is supported by AI-enabled solutions that analyse operational data, detect early signs of equipment degradation and optimise maintenance based on asset condition rather than fixed schedules.

We are also focused on helping customers make investment decisions that are future-ready. This means deploying highly efficient gas turbine technology today, while ensuring those assets can be adapted over time to utilise lower-carbon fuels such as hydrogen. The objective is not simply to add capacity, but to add capacity that is reliable, efficient and aligned with long-term decarbonisation pathways.

With global supply chain constraints on advanced turbine components such as single-crystal turbine blades, how is Mitsubishi Power ensuring timely delivery and supporting regional supply chain resilience?

From Mitsubishi Power’s perspective, the priority is to provide customers with certainty. That means strengthening production planning, improving manufacturing efficiency, and expanding capacity where needed. It also means engaging with customers early so that project timelines, component requirements and service needs can be planned with greater visibility and predictability.

In the Gulf, supply chain resilience is also supported by the region’s growing industrial base, strong logistics infrastructure, and increasing focus on local capability. Our facilities in Dammam, Saudi Arabia, and Abu Dhabi are important examples of this approach. By expanding localised repair and service capabilities through these hubs, we can support faster response times, strengthen lifecycle support for customers and contribute to national supply chain resilience objectives.
(Reporting by Anoop Menon; Editing by SA Kader)
